examples.1.1 One-page pitch: Moonshift is a cozy spatial puzzle for players 9 and up on PC and tablet. You play B.E.E.P., a repair bot restoring a six-room lunar outpost across twelve shifts of 4–8 minutes by choosing cargo, routing air, and repairing rooms before the crew wakes. Each repair changes the base; the premium $14.99 game is a weekend-sized builder that ships in nine months after a six-week demo.
examples.1.2 High concept: Moonshift plays like Unpacking's tidy spatial satisfaction crossed with the resource pressure of a one-room survival game, wrapped in a toy-like lunar diorama. B.E.E.P. has twelve shifts to turn a silent outpost into a breathing home: salvage cargo, reroute air, and watch each repaired room light up before the crew arrives. Every repaired room brings another crew radio voice back online.
examples.1.3 Design pillars: Legible first means every fault reads from the default camera through shape, colour, and glow. We will spend a week on the air-gauge animation and keep the leak rule on the board; we will not hide it in a help menu. When design proposed a hover tooltip, this pillar cut it in review.
examples.1.4 Non-goals and scope boundaries: Moonshift is not an open-world builder, a survival game, or a live service: the outpost is one fixed map, air is a puzzle resource, and there is no store or daily login. Four part-time people have twelve weeks and USD 2,000 to reach the demo, so the ranked cut list already drops online co-op and a second biome.
examples.1.5 Target audience and motivations: Our primary player is Mina, 34, who plays 25-minute puzzle sessions on an iPad after work and wants a clear win without punishment. Our secondary player is a parent co-playing with a 9-year-old who needs read-aloud radio lines, 18 px text, and a fail state that never shames. Both are served by assist mode, remapping, and colour-blind status icons.
examples.1.6 Market and competitive landscape: Outlanders is the closest comp at USD 10 on PC and Apple Arcade: we borrow its toy-diorama camera and warm palette, but avoid its mobile-style timer loops. Unlike Unpacking or Mini Motorways, Moonshift makes the air network itself the puzzle, so the empty quadrant is calm pressure at one-room scale. A launch price of USD 14.99 sits above Outlanders and below Unpacking.
examples.1.7 Platform and business model: Moonshift launches premium at USD 14.99 on Steam and iPad, with a Switch port only if the game clears 15,000 wishlists. There are no ads, currency packs, or energy timers; one six-shift expansion is planned only if the base game sells 20,000 copies. The demo ships two shifts and carries saves into the full game.
examples.1.8 References and inspiration: From Outlanders we steal the chunky diorama scale and warm sand palette, but not its characters, buildings, or UI layout. Wall-E gives us lonely-machine care through small gestures, never its plot or branded robot; Apollo 13 logs give us calm procedure and checklists, never real call signs. The mood board collects warm lunar outposts, chunky props, and long shadows.
examples.1.9 Success metrics and risks: The demo target is 70% of starts reaching shift 3, a median 90 seconds to first repair, and under 2.5 attempts per room, measured by build telemetry from the first 200 players. The top risk is a shift-4 difficulty spike; we playtest room 4 weekly and add a skip after three fails. A second risk is touch imprecision, tested by a tablet prototype in week 2.
